summary: This memo defines managed objects for an SNMPv2 entity acting as both a manager and an agent, which supports one manager reporting to another. It is historic.

eli5.summary: Some systems both ask questions and answer them. This paper helps managers share information with each other. It is historic.

questions: what is a threshold in snmp
subtitle: Managing SNMP management stations that report to other stations.

tldr.problem: Large networks need distributed management where multiple management stations coordinate with each other. A management station should be able to act both as an agent (answering queries) and as a manager (asking other stations for information).
tldr.mechanism: This MIB module defines objects for threshold-based alarms, events triggered by those alarms, and notifications sent between management stations. It allows one SNMPv2 entity to request management services from another and receive reports about network conditions.
tldr.outcome: The module is Historic, as SNMPv3 and newer management frameworks have superseded the SNMPv2 party-based administrative model on which this MIB depends.

facts.label: Supported variable types
facts.value: Integer32, Counter32, Gauge32, TimeTicks, Counter64, UInteger32

today: RFC 1451 is Historic, as it depends on the SNMPv2 party-based administrative model defined in RFC 1351, which itself is obsolete. SNMPv3, defined in RFC 3411 and related RFCs, uses a different user-based security model and does not rely on the party concept. Modern SNMP deployments using SNMPv3 would use alternative approaches for distributed management and threshold monitoring.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
A management station is an SNMP entity that monitors and controls network devices through their management information. Normally, management flows in one direction: from a station to the agents it manages. In larger networks, it is useful for one management station to request services from another, allowing distributed management across multiple stations. One station may specialize in monitoring certain parts of the network, while another coordinates overall management activities.

RFC 1451 defines a Management Information Base (MIB) module that allows a SNMPv2 entity acting in a dual role (both as a manager and as an agent) to provide services to other management stations. This enables distributed, scalable management solutions for very large networks or networks spanning multiple administrative domains.
sections.eli5: A management station is like a principal who controls the school. This MIB lets one principal ask another principal for information and help managing the network.

sections.title: Alarms, Events, and Notifications
sections.content:
The MIB defines three core concepts for manager-to-manager communication. An alarm is a condition detected by periodically sampling a network variable and checking if it falls outside a configured threshold range. For example, an alarm might trigger when CPU usage exceeds 90 percent. Each alarm condition generates an event, and each event can cause one or more notifications to be sent to other management stations using SNMPv2 Inform-Request PDUs.

The MIB organizes these concepts into three main tables: the Alarm Table (defining which variables to monitor and at what thresholds), the Event Table (specifying what events should occur when alarms trigger), and the Notification Table (routing events to appropriate management stations). This separation allows flexible configuration of what to monitor and who should be notified.
sections.eli5: You set a rule like 'warn me when the CPU goes above 90 percent.' When that happens, an event fires, and a message goes to the manager who needs to know.

sections.title: The Alarm Table and Threshold Monitoring
sections.content:
The Alarm Table is the core of the MIB. Each entry defines a periodic sampling query to monitor a specific variable at a specified interval. Only variables that are integers (Integer32, Counter32, Gauge32, TimeTicks, Counter64, or UInteger32) may be sampled. The table stores two types of thresholds: a rising threshold and a falling threshold, implementing a hysteresis mechanism to prevent rapid on-off cycling.

For each sampled variable, the entry specifies the monitoring interval (in seconds), the sample type (absolute value or delta—the change since the last sample), and the threshold values. When a sample crosses a rising threshold, a rising alarm is generated. When it crosses a falling threshold, a falling alarm is generated. Once an alarm fires, another is not generated until the opposite threshold is crossed, preventing spurious repetition.
sections.eli5: You pick a network variable to watch, say how many packets arrive per minute. You set a high limit and a low limit. If packets jump above high, you get an alert. You don't get another alert until packets drop below low, then jump above high again.

sections.title: Access Control and Distributed Queries
sections.content:
When a management station samples a variable through an Alarm Table entry, it issues a SNMPv2 request to retrieve the variable's value. This request is authenticated and optionally protected from disclosure according to the source and destination parties specified in the MIB. Access control is enforced such that a requesting management station can only create Alarm entries for variables it has permission to access.

The MIB view (the set of accessible objects) for a management station is configured to include only the Alarm entries corresponding to contexts it can access. This ensures that the Alarm mechanism does not bypass the existing SNMPv2 access control model, even though one management station is polling another. The dual role of a station (both manager and agent) is transparently managed through party contexts and view restrictions.
sections.eli5: A manager can only ask about devices it has permission to monitor. The security rules prevent a manager from sneaking access to forbidden devices through the alarm system.
